words.definition: the continuous movement and storage of water among the atmosphere, land, oceans and living organisms
words.example: The hydrological cycle transfers water through evaporation, precipitation and runoff.

words.definition: the area of land from which water flows into a particular river and its tributaries
words.example: Rain falling within a drainage basin eventually contributes to river discharge or storage.

words.definition: a highland boundary separating neighbouring drainage basins
words.example: A mountain ridge can form a watershed between two river systems.

words.definition: water falling from the atmosphere as rain, snow, sleet or hail
words.example: Heavy precipitation can rapidly increase river discharge.

words.definition: capture and temporary storage of precipitation by vegetation or other surfaces
words.example: Forest canopies intercept some rainfall before it reaches the ground.

words.definition: movement of water from the ground surface into soil
words.example: Compacted urban soil often has a lower infiltration rate.

words.definition: downward movement of water through soil and porous rock
words.example: Percolation can recharge groundwater stores.

words.definition: water flowing over the land surface toward streams and rivers
words.example: Impermeable pavement increases surface runoff after storms.

words.definition: lateral movement of water through soil toward a stream or slope outlet
words.example: Throughflow can deliver rainwater to a river after infiltration.

words.definition: water stored below ground in pores and fractures of soil and rock
words.example: Many communities pump groundwater for drinking and irrigation.

words.definition: a permeable body of rock or sediment that stores and transmits groundwater
words.example: A sandstone aquifer can supply wells over a large region.

words.definition: the upper surface of the saturated groundwater zone
words.example: The water table may fall during prolonged drought.

words.definition: combined transfer of water to the atmosphere by evaporation and plant transpiration
words.example: Evapotranspiration is often high in warm, well-vegetated regions.

words.definition: conversion of liquid water into water vapour
words.example: High temperature and wind can increase evaporation from reservoirs.

words.definition: loss of water vapour from plants, mainly through leaf stomata
words.example: Trees return large quantities of soil water to the atmosphere through transpiration.

words.definition: the volume of water flowing past a point in a river per unit time
words.example: River discharge usually rises after intense rainfall.

words.definition: the average period that matter remains stored in a particular reservoir
words.example: Groundwater in deep aquifers can have a very long residence time.

words.definition: water containing very low concentrations of dissolved salts
words.example: Lakes, rivers and groundwater contain only a small fraction of Earth's freshwater.

words.definition: water containing a high concentration of dissolved salts
words.example: Most of Earth's water is saline water in the oceans.

words.definition: large-scale ocean circulation driven by differences in seawater density caused by temperature and salinity
words.example: Thermohaline circulation redistributes heat and dissolved substances around the planet.

words.definition: a condition in which available freshwater is insufficient to meet human and ecosystem needs
words.example: Population growth and drought can intensify water scarcity.

words.definition: shortage caused by an actual lack of available freshwater relative to demand
words.example: Arid regions may experience physical water scarcity when rivers and aquifers cannot meet demand.

words.definition: limited access to water caused mainly by inadequate infrastructure, investment or institutions
words.example: A region may have rainfall but still face economic water scarcity if supply systems are poor.

words.definition: pressure on water resources when demand approaches or exceeds available supply or quality limits
words.example: High irrigation demand can create severe water stress during dry seasons.

words.definition: reliable access to sufficient safe water while protecting people and ecosystems from water-related risks
words.example: Diversified supplies and efficient use can improve water security.

words.definition: the amount of accessible freshwater present for ecological and human use
words.example: Climate variability affects freshwater availability from year to year.

words.definition: water removed from a river, lake, reservoir or aquifer for human use
words.example: Agriculture accounts for a large share of global water withdrawals.

words.definition: withdrawn water that is evaporated, incorporated into products or otherwise not returned quickly to its source
words.example: Irrigated crops can cause high water consumption through evapotranspiration.

words.definition: artificial application of water to crops or soil
words.example: Drip irrigation can reduce water losses compared with flood irrigation.

words.definition: long-term reduction of groundwater storage because extraction exceeds recharge
words.example: Intensive pumping for agriculture can cause groundwater depletion.

words.definition: addition of water to groundwater storage through infiltration and percolation
words.example: Wet seasons provide natural aquifer recharge in many regions.

words.definition: removal of dissolved salts from seawater or brackish water to produce freshwater
words.example: Desalination can increase supply but requires substantial energy.

words.definition: collection and storage of rainfall for later use
words.example: Roof tanks allow households to practice rainwater harvesting.

words.definition: an artificial or natural body of stored water used for supply, energy or flow regulation
words.example: A reservoir can provide drinking water during dry periods.

words.definition: a barrier built across a river to store water or control flow
words.example: A large dam may improve water supply while disrupting sediment transport and fish migration.

words.definition: the total freshwater used directly and indirectly to produce goods, services or consumption patterns
words.japanese: ウォーターフットプリント
words.example: Meat production often has a larger water footprint than many plant foods.

words.definition: water used to produce a commodity and effectively transferred through trade when that commodity is exchanged
words.example: Importing grain can allow a dry country to import virtual water.

words.definition: water resources shared across political borders
words.example: International cooperation is important for managing transboundary water in shared river basins.

words.definition: disagreement or tension over access to, control of or impacts on water resources
words.example: Competing upstream and downstream demands can contribute to water conflict.

words.definition: coordinated management of water, land and related resources to balance social, economic and ecosystem needs
words.example: Integrated water resource management considers agriculture, cities and river ecosystems together.

words.definition: harvesting wild aquatic organisms from natural ecosystems
words.example: Ocean tuna fleets operate as capture fisheries.

words.definition: farming of aquatic organisms such as fish, shellfish or algae under managed conditions
words.example: Aquaculture now supplies a large share of fish consumed globally.

words.definition: a population or management unit of fish exploited or monitored as a resource
words.example: Managers estimate fish stock size before setting catch limits.

words.definition: the largest long-term catch that can theoretically be taken without reducing a population's productive capacity
words.example: Fishing near maximum sustainable yield requires reliable stock estimates.

words.definition: harvesting fish faster than populations can replace themselves
words.example: Overfishing can reduce breeding populations and alter food webs.

words.definition: the amount of fishing activity, often measured by vessels, gear, time or capacity
words.example: Reducing fishing effort can help depleted stocks recover.

words.definition: non-target organisms unintentionally caught during fishing
words.example: Sea turtles may be killed as bycatch in some longline fisheries.

words.definition: fishing by dragging a net across or near the seafloor
words.example: Bottom trawling can damage benthic habitats.

words.definition: a large surrounding net that closes underneath a school of fish
words.example: Purse seine fishing is commonly used for schooling tuna.

words.definition: fishing with a long main line carrying many baited hooks
words.example: Longline fishing can catch seabirds and sharks as bycatch.

words.definition: a legal limit on the quantity of a stock that may be harvested
words.example: A fishery quota can restrict total catch during the season.

words.definition: a defined ocean or coastal zone managed to conserve ecosystems or species
words.example: A no-take marine protected area can allow fish biomass to increase.

words.definition: scientific estimation of fish population size, structure and fishing pressure
words.example: Stock assessment data are used to revise catch limits.

words.definition: a chain of indirect ecological effects caused by changes at one trophic level
words.example: Removing large predators can trigger a trophic cascade through a marine ecosystem.

words.definition: protein-rich feed ingredient produced from processed fish or fish by-products
words.example: Some aquaculture systems depend heavily on fishmeal.

words.definition: the amount of feed required to produce a unit increase in farmed animal mass
words.example: A lower feed conversion ratio generally indicates more efficient production.

words.definition: farming species from different trophic levels so that wastes from one become resources for another
words.example: Seaweed can absorb nutrients released by fish in integrated multi-trophic aquaculture.

words.definition: replacement of mangrove habitat by another land or water use
words.example: Shrimp ponds have caused mangrove conversion in some tropical coasts.

words.definition: aquatic food produced or harvested in ways intended to maintain stocks and minimize ecosystem damage
words.example: Consumers may choose certified sustainable seafood to reduce pressure on overfished stocks.

words.definition: independent assessment and labeling of fisheries against specified sustainability standards
words.example: Fishery certification can give markets information about harvesting practices.

words.definition: contamination released from a clearly identifiable location such as a pipe or outlet
words.example: Effluent from a factory pipe is point-source pollution.

words.definition: diffuse contamination originating from many scattered sources across a landscape
words.example: Fertilizer washed from many fields creates non-point-source pollution.

words.definition: wastewater containing human excreta and other domestic wastes
words.example: Untreated sewage can introduce pathogens and nutrients into rivers.

words.definition: physical, biological and chemical processes used to remove contaminants from used water
words.example: Wastewater treatment reduces organic matter before effluent is discharged.

words.definition: the amount of dissolved oxygen microorganisms require to decompose biodegradable organic matter in water
words.japanese: 生物化学的酸素要求量（BOD）
words.example: High biochemical oxygen demand can indicate strong organic pollution.

words.definition: molecular oxygen present in water and available to aquatic organisms
words.example: Fish may die when dissolved oxygen falls to very low levels.

words.definition: nutrient enrichment of water that stimulates excessive biological production and can deplete oxygen
words.example: Fertilizer runoff can cause eutrophication in lakes.

words.definition: rapid growth and accumulation of algae or cyanobacteria in water
words.example: A nutrient-rich lake may develop a dense algal bloom in summer.

words.definition: an area of water with oxygen levels too low to support most aerobic organisms
words.japanese: 貧酸素水域・デッドゾーン
words.example: Decomposition of algal biomass can create a coastal dead zone.

words.definition: excessive input of nutrients, especially nitrogen and phosphorus, into water bodies
words.example: Nutrient pollution from farms can stimulate algal growth.

words.definition: harmful change in water temperature caused by human activity
words.example: Warm cooling water from a power station can cause thermal pollution.

words.definition: a dense metallic element that can be toxic to organisms at elevated concentrations
words.example: Mercury is a heavy metal that can accumulate in food webs.

words.definition: movement of agricultural pest-control chemicals from land into surface water
words.example: Heavy rain can carry pesticide runoff into streams.

words.definition: plastic particles generally smaller than five millimetres
words.japanese: マイクロプラスチック
words.example: Microplastics are now found in rivers, oceans and aquatic organisms.

words.definition: release of petroleum into an aquatic or terrestrial environment
words.example: An oil spill can coat seabirds and damage coastal habitats.

words.definition: increase in contaminant concentration at successively higher trophic levels
words.japanese: 生物濃縮（栄養段階上昇による）
words.example: Mercury can biomagnify from plankton to large predatory fish.

words.definition: progressive build-up of a substance in an organism because uptake exceeds elimination
words.example: A persistent pesticide may bioaccumulate in an animal's tissues over time.

words.definition: a species whose presence, absence or condition provides information about environmental quality
words.example: Sensitive aquatic insects can serve as indicator species of clean water.

words.definition: a combined numerical score based on several measurements of water condition
words.example: A water quality index can summarize oxygen, pH, nutrients and other variables.

words.definition: action taken to remove, contain or reduce environmental contamination
words.example: Wetland plants can sometimes assist remediation of polluted water.
